title: The Bible’s Hardest Sexual Stories Were Never Written to Entertain You—They Were Written to Expose You
paragraphs: The Bible’s Hardest Sexual Stories Were Never Written to Entertain You—They Were Written to Expose You

David took another man’s wife. Judah slept with a woman he thought was a prostitute. Tamar entered a desperate sexual scandal. Samson repeatedly confused desire with love. A woman caught in adultery was dragged before Jesus and publicly shamed. Scripture refuses to sanitize any of it. But if you think these stories are mainly about “those terrible people back then,” you may have missed the most frightening—and beautiful—reason God allowed them to remain in the Bible.
There are passages in the Bible we love to underline.
And then there are passages we quietly hope nobody asks us about.
The Psalms make their way onto coffee mugs.
John 3:16 appears on signs and shirts.
But nobody decorates the living room with Genesis 38.
Nobody sends newlyweds a greeting card featuring David, Bathsheba, and Uriah.
Nobody casually says, “For tonight’s family devotional, let’s talk about Judah and Tamar.”
Some biblical stories are uncomfortable because Scripture is brutally unwilling to pretend that human beings are cleaner than we really are.
And consequences that sometimes ripple through generations.
And perhaps that is precisely why we need these stories.

Because God did not give us a Bible filled exclusively with polished saints standing heroically beneath heavenly spotlights. He gave us a Bible populated by human beings whose lives sometimes look disturbingly familiar.
Not because God celebrates their sin.
Because God tells the truth about it.
And underneath some of Scripture's darkest sexual stories is a question that eventually stops being about David, Judah, Tamar, Samson, or the woman standing terrified before an angry crowd.
What does God see when He looks into the rooms of my life that nobody else enters?
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because sexual sin rarely begins where everybody can see it.
Jesus took His listeners somewhere much deeper.

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27–28).
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn

The idea is not merely noticing that another human being is physically attractive. The construction points toward looking in order to desire—the intentional cultivation of lust. The gaze becomes more than sight; it becomes the deliberate feeding of desire.
Jesus moves the battlefield from the bedroom to the heart.
That destroys one of our favorite hiding places.
And suddenly the Bible's scandalous stories are no longer ancient gossip.
This was not some pagan king who had never encountered God.
The man who had stood before Goliath when almost everyone else was terrified.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most chilling sentences in David's biography:
One evening he walked onto the roof of his palace and saw a woman bathing.
The text identifies her clearly: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite. David therefore receives a boundary before he crosses it. She belongs within another man's marriage covenant.
Yet David sends for her anyway.
That matters because sin often gives us exits before it gives us consequences.
A spouse's face flashing through your mind.
A strange heaviness in your spirit.
A moment when you could close the browser.
David summoned Uriah home, apparently hoping Uriah would sleep with Bathsheba and later assume the child was his.
But Uriah refused the comforts of home while his fellow soldiers remained in battle.
David did not wake up one morning planning to become the kind of man who would arrange a loyal soldier's death.
That is one of sin's terrifying characteristics.
It rarely shows you the final destination when it offers you the first compromise.
The emotional affair says, “We're only talking.”
Fantasy says, “It's only happening in your head.”
Sin almost never introduces itself by saying:
“Hello. I am here to hollow out your integrity, wound the people you love, numb your conscience, damage your communion with God, and possibly destroy things you spent decades building.”
He tells David about a wealthy man with many sheep who steals the one beloved lamb belonging to a poor man.
And Nathan turns the entire story around with four devastating words:
The Hebrew is even more stark:
And Nathan answers with something almost shocking:
“The LORD also has put away your sin.”
But the story does not pretend his choices were harmless. Serious consequences remain.
That distinction is essential to biblical grace.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is not pretending nobody was wounded.
Grace is not removing accountability from abusers, adulterers, predators, exploiters, or manipulators.
Biblical forgiveness does not mean victims must deny reality, abandon wise boundaries, refuse lawful justice, or immediately restore broken trust.
God names David's evil before announcing forgiveness.
Some people want forgiveness without repentance.
Others believe their sin is too ugly for forgiveness.
And then there is Judah and Tamar.
Genesis 38 may be one of the most awkward chapters in Scripture.
Tamar had married Judah's son Er. After Er died, the family obligation passed to Onan, but Onan exploited the arrangement while deliberately refusing the responsibility attached to it.
After Onan died under God's judgment, Judah promised Tamar his younger son Shelah when he grew older.
Then Judah failed to fulfill his promise.
Eventually she disguised herself, and Judah—believing her to be a prostitute—slept with her.
When Tamar's pregnancy became known, Judah reacted with horrifying hypocrisy and demanded severe punishment.
Then Tamar produced evidence identifying the father.
The Bible is not turning deception or prostitution into virtues.
The story exposes Judah's failure, Tamar's vulnerability, the hypocrisy of sexual double standards, and the tangled consequences of covenant faithlessness.
Judah was ready to condemn publicly the very sexual scandal in which he was secretly implicated.
We condemn the person whose scandal became visible while protecting the version of ourselves nobody discovered.
We rage against somebody else's adultery while feeding pornography privately.
We criticize another person's divorce while emotionally abandoning our own spouse.
We mock someone's sexual brokenness while carefully clearing our browser history.
We demand that fallen Christians be exposed while praying nobody ever screenshots our private messages.
But Scripture keeps turning the mirror around.
And maybe that sentence hurts because somewhere inside you there is something you desperately do not want exposed.
Maybe you have become incredibly skilled at appearing spiritually healthy.
And another version of you appears.
If that sentence made your stomach tighten, do not run from Jesus.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation whispers, “Hide because God could never want you now.”
The Gospel says something entirely different.
And still He calls sinners to Himself.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She is caught in adultery and placed before Him publicly.
Adultery requires more than one participant, yet only the woman is dragged into the spectacle.
Jesus refuses to become another instrument in their hypocrisy.
After the accusers leave, He speaks to her.
But Jesus does not stop there.
No permission from Christ to remain enslaved.

A textual note is important here for readers who care about biblical accuracy: the account commonly called the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest and strongest Greek manuscript witnesses and appears in different locations in parts of the manuscript tradition. Christians should therefore be careful about building a doctrine uniquely upon this passage. Its central picture of Jesus extending mercy while calling sinners away from sin, however, is abundantly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
And that brings us to something Christianity understands that our culture desperately needs.
You are more than your sexual history.
You are also responsible for what you do with your sexuality.
Your desires are not your god.
Other people's bodies are not products.
Sex is not merely recreational chemistry.
Pornography does not become harmless because nobody physically entered the room.
And sexual holiness is not God trying to keep pleasure away from humanity.
The biblical story begins with embodied human beings created male and female and a marriage union described with the Hebrew expression:
Sexuality therefore enters Scripture not as something dirty but as something powerful enough to require covenant faithfulness.
The enemy's strategy has always been to take gifts from God and detach them from the God who gave them.
And eventually people discover that getting everything they wanted did not cure the ache underneath what they wanted.
Because sometimes what we call lust is carrying another hunger beneath it.
But it may explain why simply saying “try harder” has failed so many people.
You do not merely need stronger willpower.
This is where Jesus becomes more than a religious teacher telling sexually broken people to behave.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your habits.
He came to give you a new heart.
At the cross, Christ carries guilt without pretending guilt does not exist.
He absorbs judgment without calling sin harmless.
He offers mercy without rewriting evil as virtue.
The scandal of Christianity is not that God discovered humanity was better than expected.
The scandal is that God knew exactly what humanity was—and Christ came anyway.
David's adultery did not surprise Him.
Judah's hypocrisy did not surprise Him.
Samson's appetites did not surprise Him.
Peter's denial did not surprise Him.
Your browser history does not surprise Him.
Your affair does not surprise Him.
Your secret fantasies do not surprise Him.
Your sexual past does not surprise Him.
What happened to you does not surprise Him either.
And hear this carefully, especially if someone else's sexual sin was committed against you:
Another person's evil is not your moral stain.
Scripture's sexual stories contain sinners who need repentance, but they also contain people who were exploited, betrayed, objectified, abandoned, or violated.
Those categories must never be confused.
The wounded do not need to repent for having been wounded.
The guilty must not use “grace” to silence the wounded.
Jesus is full of compassion toward the broken, and biblical repentance requires sinners to stop hiding behind spiritual language.
Maybe that is why these difficult stories survived thousands of years.
God knew we would need them.
We would need David because some believers would fall terribly after years of walking with God.
We would need Judah because religious people would become experts at seeing everybody else's sexual failure.
We would need Tamar because vulnerable people would need to know Scripture does not simply erase them from the story.
We would need Samson because gifted people would mistake gifting for godliness.
And we would need Jesus because eventually every honest person would realize:
That is the moment the Gospel stops being theology you agree with and becomes oxygen.
You stop saying, “Jesus died for sinners.”
You stop talking about grace like a doctrine.
You fall into it like someone who has finally stopped pretending he can swim.
Repentance is not paying God back.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια — metanoia: repentance, a decisive change of mind and direction that bears fruit in a changed life.
It means bringing darkness into light.
Confessing what needs to be confessed.
Seeking accountability where secrecy has become your hiding place.
Getting pastoral and professional help where patterns have become deeply entrenched.
And refusing to call bondage “freedom” merely because culture gave it a softer name.
Jesus does not expose you because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes what is killing you because He intends to make you free.
That is why His words about lust are severe.
ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
The one intentionally looking toward lust.
He goes after the gaze because He loves the person behind the eyes.
He goes after fantasy because He wants the heart.
He goes after secret sin because He wants the whole human being.
Christ does not merely want your Sunday.
He wants the midnight version of you.
And if something inside you has been whispering while you read this—
Not after you clean yourself up.
Sometimes freedom begins with one honest sentence.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging our need for mercy is the first crack in a wall of pretending.

And if Christ has already rescued you from a sexual past you once believed would define you forever, tell your testimony. Somebody scrolling beneath this article may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
Not as a badge proving that you are holy, but as a doorway through which someone hiding in shame may encounter biblical truth and the mercy of Christ.

If you know someone whose marriage is struggling, someone fighting pornography, someone drowning in shame over their past, someone who believes Christianity has nothing to say except “you are disgusting,” or even an unbelieving friend who has never understood what Christians actually mean by grace—send this to them.
That is one simple way to glorify God: not by promoting us for our sake, but by helping His truth travel farther than it would have traveled without you.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
But before you leave, remember the strangest thing about the Bible's hardest sexual stories.
God could have edited them out.
Because the Bible was never written to convince you that God's people were flawless.
It was written to reveal a faithful God who enters the wreckage of sinful humanity and accomplishes redemption that sinners could never manufacture for themselves.
And Matthew's genealogy makes the point almost impossible to miss.
The genealogy walks through human scandal until it arrives at the Savior.
That does not make the scandals good.
God does not need to pretend your past never happened in order to redeem your future.
He does not call adultery faithfulness.
He does not call lust purity.
He does not call exploitation love.
He does not call darkness light.
He forgives those who come to Him through Christ.
He teaches wounded people that what happened to them is not the end of their story.
And He teaches guilty people that repentance is not the funeral of hope.
It may be where hope finally begins.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Why did God put such scandalous sexual stories in the Bible?”
“What if God left them there so people with scandalous stories would know they could still come home?”
The Bible's darkest stories are not permission to remain in darkness.
They are evidence that darkness does not get the final word when Jesus enters the story.
Your worst chapter may tell the truth about what happened—but only Jesus gets to write the final sentence.
